index.t007: Diligence is the mother of good luck.
index.t009:
Two independent algorithms trading on different entry rules.
  Below: results over five years of history, an honest risk assessment by
  Monte Carlo simulation, and weekly oversight rules with actions defined
  in advance.
index.t022: The mechanics are identical for both algorithms and never change from trade to trade.
index.t026:
Placed on every trade at opening,
      calculated from the instrument’s current volatility. There are no trades without a stop.
index.t028: The take-profit is fixed, set in advance for each instrument as a multiple of risk: the position closes when it is reached, and the target does not trail the price. In addition, Algorithm 1 has a time-based exit — the position is force-closed by the end of the trading day, or before the instrument’s session ends if that comes earlier, while there is still liquidity in the market. That is why it never holds trades overnight. Algorithm 2 has no time exit: a position lives until its stop or take-profit.
index.t030:
1% of the deposit per trade. Lot size is fitted
      to the width of the stop: the further the stop, the smaller the volume. So a loss
      at the stop is always 1% of the deposit, however wide that stop turns out to be.
index.t032: Not used. A losing position is never added to or reversed — it is closed at the stop.
index.t034:
One for each algorithm:
      while its trade is open, it makes no new entries on that instrument.
      The algorithms are independent, so one instrument can carry two positions
      at once, including opposing ones.
index.t036: Algorithm 1 — 3.6 hours on average, and never holds a trade longer than a day. Algorithm 2 — 10 hours on average, with 29% of trades carried overnight.
index.t037:
A fixed stop means the loss on a single trade is capped at 1% of the deposit.
  The exception is a price gap at the market open: if price jumps over the stop level,
  the loss will be larger than calculated. Algorithm 2, which carries positions
  overnight, is exposed to this risk; Algorithm 1 almost never is.
index.t039: Percent of deposit at 1% risk per trade, without reinvestment: this is an arithmetic sum of results, not compound interest. 983% over five years (about 16% a month on average) — more in some months, negative in others. The curve is built from closed trades.
index.t055: 57 of 61 months are profitable. Four are negative: January 2022 (−12.2%), August 2024 (−7.0%), November 2021 (−2.4%) and January 2023 (−1.5%). The worst of them is January 2022. The best month was January 2024, +42.5%. The average across all months is +16.1%.
index.t060: Separately, Algorithm 2 drew down 17.6% and Algorithm 1 13.0%, summing to 30.6%. The portfolio drawdown is 17.6%: risk is dampened because the algorithms lose on different days. This is measured, not asserted — across 556 days of joint trading both were negative 144 times against 153 expected by chance.
index.t062: Everything shown above is calculated on balance — on closed trades. But while a position is open the account fluctuates, and the screen shows a different figure — equity, the funds together with the floating result. Its drawdown is deeper, and it is equity that you will see in your own account.
index.a189: Drawdown on balance and on equity
index.t065: On closed trades the account drew down 17.6%, on equity — 22.6%: deeper by a factor of 1.29. Sampling is hourly, 31 thousand readings per source.
index.t067: The equity drawdown is 5.0% deeper than the balance one — the gap between 22.6% and 17.6%. You would expect a floating loss to explain it: open positions go negative, the account sinks further. But over five years the floating loss never once exceeded 1.9% of the deposit — almost three times less than what would be needed. So where does the rest come from? Let us take apart the worst episode.
index.t074: Here is the answer: the depth came not from a floating loss, but from floating profit at the moment of the peak. In July the account stood at 584% on closed trades, and open positions showed a further +6.6%. The terminal read 591% — but those six percent were on the screen, not in the pocket. Then the balance fell by 15.5%, the unrealised profit evaporated, and from its high the account came down to 569%.
index.t076:
This is the whole gap between the two curves: above zero the open positions
  are in profit, below zero at a loss.
index.t077: 84% of the time the floating result is non-negative — positions are either in profit or closed. The upward peaks run far higher than the dips: up to +10.4% against −1.9%. It is exactly this asymmetry that creates inflated highs, from which the drawdown is then measured.
index.t078: Hence the practical conclusion. On a good day the figure in the terminal is inflated by unrealised profit, and when that goes it feels as though more has been lost than really was. Knowing this quantity matters so you are not frightened in the moment. And the control thresholds are set on balance: the watcher measures a hundred closed trades, and the alarm must trigger on the same thing that is being measured.
index.t080: History happened to run in one particular order of trades. To see how much the result depends on that order, we shuffled it 20,000 times and looked at what came out.
index.t081: How the account might have gone
index.t082:
The same 3,291 trades arranged in a different order. In red — what actually
  happened; dashed — the median of all variants.
index.t087: The ends converge for a reason: shuffling changes the order but not the set of trades, so every variant finishes at the same total. The spread lives in the middle of the road — and it is moderate: against an actual +452% at the halfway mark, the simulated variants fall within a corridor from +402% to +582%.
index.t088: For drawdown the reference point is this: a median of 24.5%, and that is what you should plan around. A drawdown deeper than 30% appeared in 18.1% of the recalculations, deeper than 40% — in 2.1%.
index.t090: How to read the table. On the left is the drawdown level in percent of the deposit; in the middle, the share out of twenty thousand recalculations where the account went deeper; on the right, how long such a drawdown lasted. Deeper than 40% went 427 variants out of twenty thousand, deeper than 50% — forty-one, deeper than 60% — two. The last row is empty for a reason: not one of the twenty thousand variants went deeper than 70%, the heaviest reached 63.0%.
index.t105:
A subscriber can halve both the return and the drawdown by taking
    a half copy multiplier — they scale together.
index.t106: Three months without a new high is normal, not a breakdown. Knowing this in advance matters: it is in the fourth month of a drawdown that the worst decisions get made.
index.t120:
From 1:100. No more than seven positions are
      open at once, and half the time no more than two, so the margin is ample.
      At 1:500 the deposit load never exceeds 10%.
index.t122: Hedging is mandatory, not netting. The algorithms are independent and may hold opposing positions on one instrument; on a netting account the second trade would close the first, and the result would diverge from the strategy. Execution is market; the instruments are ordinary: currency pairs, gold, indices, oil.
index.t124:
Return and drawdown
      scale together. A half multiplier gives half of both —
      it is a way to fit the risk to yourself. But remember: as you reduce
      the risk, raise the deposit according to the table above — otherwise some positions will go
      at the minimum lot with inflated risk, and the reduction will be illusory.
index.t125: On divergence of results. Copies open at current market prices, so your result will not match the strategy exactly — the difference accumulates from spread and slippage on every trade. At a flow of about 60 trades a month this is a noticeable amount, and the smaller the account, the larger it is in percentage terms. A deposit from $1,000 and a stable connection reduce the divergence; removing it entirely is impossible.
index.t127:
Two numbers are checked every week. Drawdown answers the question “how much
  does it hurt right now”; expectancy over the last 100 trades answers “is the system
  still working”. The actions are defined in advance, before things get unpleasant.
index.t128: Oversight is run by a separate watcher algorithm, not by a person acting on mood. It runs on the same server, reads the account history, recalculates every metric weekly — for the portfolio as a whole, for each of the two algorithms and for each instrument separately — and compares them against the thresholds in the table below. It separately reconciles the actual number of trades against the expected one: this is how a stopped or hung algorithm is detected, which would otherwise look simply like a prolonged drawdown.
index.t129:
The watcher makes no trading decisions
  and never intervenes in trades — it only measures and reports. Its logic
  has been checked against the full five-year history: the drawdown threshold was never reached,
  and the expectancy alarm fired twice — both times right at the boundary, and both times
  a review would have shown the system operating normally. On simulated deep
  drawdowns the warning arrives a month to six weeks before the critical level.
index.t137: check that all algorithms are running
index.t143: Expectancy over the last 100 trades, % of deposit per trade
index.t146: The alarm threshold is expectancy below −0.05% per trade. The watcher checks against it once a week: across 254 weekly checks the alarm fired once — on 2 Feb 2022, expectancy −0.084%. The average across all readings is +0.30%.
index.t147:
What happened next: the following hundred trades came out
  profitable, and expectancy returned to its average without any action at all.
  An alarm is not an order to stop but a demand to investigate: to check whether all
  algorithms are running, whether one has hung, whether the instruments have changed behaviour.
  A review would have shown the system operating normally.
index.t148: The curve on the chart is continuous — it is recalculated after every trade rather than weekly, and it touched the threshold more often: 3 episodes over five years, the deepest at −0.112%. Only one of them survived to the day of the weekly check. We show this openly, so that a line beneath the threshold does not look like a contradiction of the text: the weekly control step is a deliberate choice, it damps out short spikes that there is nothing to be done about.
index.t149: There are deliberately no intermediate thresholds. Over five years expectancy fell to zero 17 times, and the following hundred trades after that were never once unprofitable — from +0.19% to +0.56% per trade against a historical average of +0.25%; in 11 cases out of 16, better than average. Reacting to such dips would mean trading against a reversion to the mean.
index.t150: Parameters are not changed during a drawdown. The settings were fitted on the entire available history of the instruments — six to seven years — while a drawdown is an event spanning a hundred trades. Changing parameters inside one means fitting the system to a random stretch.
index.t151: What the result is made of
index.t154: colour — which algorithm; an instrument traded by both appears twice
index.t170: A row is one instrument for one algorithm, and the marker colour shows which. Three instruments are traded by both algorithms and therefore appear in the list twice: XAUUSD, NZDUSD and USTEC.
index.t171: The average RR column together with the win rate reveals the mechanics of a source. Gold takes 6.44 per unit of risk at a 20% win rate — rarely, but in large amounts; oil is the opposite, 0.73 at a 71% win rate — often and in small amounts. Both designs are profitable but behave in opposite ways, and they fall into drawdown at different times.
index.t172: Note the drawdowns: the individual drawdown of a source does not add up into the portfolio one — the sum of all sixteen would be 141%, while the portfolio drew down 17.6%.
index.t173: Gold brings in the most: +249% from Algorithm 2 and +88% from Algorithm 1, together a third of the entire result. The dependence on it is softened by the fact that these are two different algorithms with different entry rules — not one bet doubled in size.
index.t174: The outer periods are shorter than the rest — the history begins in August 2021 and ends in August 2026. Counted as full years from the start, the spread is even: +142%, +205%, +232%, +180%, +218% — all five are profitable, and none accounts for more than a quarter of the total. The result does not rest on a single lucky year.
index.t175: The average win is 2.35% of the deposit against an average loss of 0.98% — a ratio of 2.39 at a share of profitable trades of 38.4%.
index.t177: This is the strategy’s debut on the platform. The historical calculation exists; live statistics are only beginning — and accumulating them is the main task right now. The goal for the coming year: to build up a full body of live trading statistics that can be presented not as words but as an export from the platform.
index.t178: That is why the fee is below market at the moment. The usual rate for copy trading is 25–30% of profit; a strategy without a public track record has no right to ask for that much. As statistics accumulate the rate will rise — but only for new subscribers: the terms of an existing subscription do not change once it has been set up. Whoever joins at the start stays on the starting terms.
index.t179: Work on the system continues. The set of instruments is not frozen: each new one goes through the same selection — a stability check across the two halves of history, a test against randomness, an assessment of execution costs. Whatever fails is not added, even if it looks profitable. A third algorithm with independent entry logic is in development.
index.t180:
Every expansion of the set has reduced the portfolio’s
  drawdown rather than increasing it: instruments are chosen so that they lose
  in different periods. That is the point of adding new ones — not so much a rise
  in return as a smoothing of the dips.
index.t182:
Everything set out here is a calculation on historical data, not the result of live
  trading. History describes the past; the future may turn out differently, and the actual
  drawdown may exceed 41%. Live statistics are only starting to accumulate —
  and they are what should be treated as the main evidence once they exist.
index.t183:
The algorithms are independent in their results, but not entirely independent
  in their design. A market regime in which both draw down simultaneously is theoretically
  possible. In five years of history this has never happened: there is not a single month
  out of 61 in which both would have ended negative.
index.t184:
Copying is executed at current market prices, so a subscriber’s result
  will differ from the strategy’s. On accounts smaller than $1,000 the
  divergence is noticeably larger because of rounding in position size.

index.t111: It depends on the risk you choose. The lower the risk per trade, the smaller the position size — and the sooner it runs into the smallest lot the broker allows. What happens next is not what it looks like: the trade still opens, but at the minimum lot, and its risk turns out larger than the one you set. You will think you are risking 0.25%, while on some instruments the risk will be two or three times that.
